domain: Public Health Policy / Criminal Justice / Political Economy
topic_summary: Analysis of drug policy frameworks examining prohibition, harm-reduction, and legalization as competing readings of the substance-control kernel. Each reading instantiates fundamentally different constraints with distinct victim sets: users as criminals (prohibition), users as public health cases (harm-reduction), or third parties bearing externality costs (legalization).

key_entities: Public health system (treatment providers, harm reduction services)
Third-party victims (impaired driving victims, secondhand harm)
Communities affected by enforcement (disproportionately marginalized populations)
Tax revenue recipients (state budgets under legalization models)
key_tensions: Individual autonomy vs paternalistic state protection
Public health frame vs criminal justice frame for substance use
Black market violence vs legal market externalities
key_mechanisms: Criminal prohibition enforcement (arrests, incarceration, asset forfeiture)
Harm reduction service provision (needle exchange, supervised consumption, naloxone distribution)
Regulatory taxation and licensing (legal market controls)
Price signaling via illegality premium vs taxation
key_absences: Supply-side dynamics beyond simple 'criminal organization' framing—structural economic incentives, global production chains
Enforcement selectivity mechanisms—who actually faces criminalization within the 'users as criminals' frame

axes.human_readable: Prohibition Reading: Users as Criminals, State as Moral Enforcer
axes.structural_delta: Substance use defined as moral transgression warranting criminal sanction; state authority grounded in protecting moral order and deterring harm through punishment
axes.primary_observable: Incarceration rates for possession offenses; enforcement spending relative to treatment spending; sentencing severity for drug crimes
axes.selection_reason: Core reading instantiating criminalization constraint; highest extractiveness; distinct victim set from other readings

reading_metadata.commitment: Substance use is moral transgression requiring state punishment to protect social order
reading_metadata.authority_grounding: Moral majoritarian mandate; state as guardian of public virtue
reading_metadata.expected_structural_delta: Users enter criminal victim set; enforcement becomes primary state response; black market emerges as secondary constraint

axes.human_readable: Harm Reduction Reading: Users as Public Health Cases, State as Service Provider
axes.structural_delta: Substance use defined as health condition requiring medical intervention; state authority grounded in minimizing morbidity and mortality through service provision without requiring abstinence
axes.primary_observable: Overdose death rates; infectious disease transmission rates among users; service accessibility metrics (needle exchange coverage, supervised consumption site availability)
axes.selection_reason: Intermediate reading reframing constraint from criminal to medical; coordination mechanism without full legalization; distinct observable from prohibition and legalization

reading_metadata.commitment: Substance use is health condition requiring pragmatic intervention to reduce harm, independent of use cessation
reading_metadata.authority_grounding: Public health expertise; epidemiological evidence base
reading_metadata.expected_structural_delta: Users exit criminal victim set but remain subject to paternalistic health intervention; enforcement recedes but does not disappear; supply chain remains criminalized

axes.human_readable: Legalization Reading: Users as Autonomous Consumers, Third Parties as Victims
axes.structural_delta: Substance use defined as individual choice with externality costs; state authority grounded in regulating market to internalize harms to third parties while respecting user autonomy
axes.primary_observable: Legal market tax revenue; DUI and impairment-related harm rates; regulatory compliance costs; price elasticity effects on consumption
axes.selection_reason: Opposing reading shifting victim set from users to third parties; introduces market mechanisms and tax extraction; highest structural distinctiveness from prohibition

reading_metadata.commitment: Substance use is individual liberty issue; state intervenes only to prevent third-party harm and capture externality costs via taxation
reading_metadata.authority_grounding: Liberal autonomy principles; market efficiency; fiscal pragmatism
reading_metadata.expected_structural_delta: Users exit victim set entirely; third parties enter victim set via externalities; black market collapses; state becomes revenue beneficiary via taxation; legal industry emerges as new beneficiary

axes.structural_delta: Within prohibition framework, enforcement concentrates on marginalized populations despite use patterns across demographics
axes.primary_observable: Arrest rates by race, income, geography relative to survey-reported use rates; stop-and-frisk patterns; sentencing disparities
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: structural consequence of prohibition reading rather than independent reading of kernel; important omega dimension

axes.human_readable: Supply Chain Constraint Persistence Across Readings
axes.structural_delta: Production and distribution constraints persist across all three readings but with different enforcement targets and violence levels
axes.primary_observable: Cartel violence rates; corruption indices; legal pharmaceutical capture; agricultural source country impacts
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: upstream mountain affecting all readings but not itself a reading of the substance-control kernel; supply-side rather than demand-side frame

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Enforcement concentrates on marginalized populations despite use pattern uniformity
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Structural consequence of prohibition reading rather than independent kernel reading; captured implicitly in prohibition's victim specification but warrants omega treatment for enforcement targeting mechanism

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Production and distribution constraints persist with different violence/corruption levels across readings
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Upstream constraint affecting all readings but not itself a reading of substance-control kernel; supply-side dimension orthogonal to demand-side user-status question

omegas.description: Prohibition reading's victim set is theoretically 'all users' but enforcement concentrates on marginalized populations. Is this a separate Snare or intrinsic to prohibition's ε? Enforcement selectivity mechanism may warrant independent axis treatment.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + deferred axis enforcement_selectivity

omegas.description: Many jurisdictions operate hybrid regimes (decriminalized possession + criminalized supply). Does this represent stable intermediate reading or incoherent overlay of prohibition + harm-reduction? Structural stability unclear.

Can societies transition directly prohibition→legalization or must they pass through harm-reduction? Path dependency may constrain reading adoption sequence. Historical evidence mixed (Portugal vs Uruguay vs Canada).

Is supply_chain_constraint_persistence a true Mountain (agricultural/chemical production constraints) or Piton of policy choice? Legalization suggests Piton—production feasibility demonstrated—but international treaty architecture may create Mountain-like rigidity.

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: supply_chain_constraint_persistence classified as mountain but legalization evidence suggests production feasibility (Piton of prohibition rather than Mountain of chemistry/agriculture). Generated omega_supply_chain_reclassification to bound this uncertainty. No F34 despite complex policy domain—readings are well-documented in comparative policy literature.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The substance-control kernel: what grounds state authority to regulate individual substance use and how should that authority be exercised
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Contested across three incompatible grounds: moral majority mandate (prohibition), public health expertise (harm-reduction), liberal autonomy principles (legalization)
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Constitutional Succession (competing legitimate interpretive frameworks without shared meta-rule for adjudication)

readings.commitment: Substance use is moral transgression requiring state punishment to protect social order
readings.authority_grounding: Moral majoritarian mandate; state as guardian of public virtue
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users enter criminal victim set (ε_high); enforcement apparatus becomes primary beneficiary; black market violence emerges as secondary externality; state exercises coercive rather than service-provision authority

readings.commitment: Substance use is health condition requiring pragmatic intervention to reduce harm, independent of use cessation
readings.authority_grounding: Public health expertise; epidemiological evidence base
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users exit criminal victim set but remain subject to paternalistic health intervention (ε_mod); enforcement recedes but supply chain remains criminalized; overdose and disease transmission become primary observables; state shifts to service provider role

readings.commitment: Substance use is individual liberty issue; state intervenes only to prevent third-party harm and capture externality costs
readings.authority_grounding: Liberal autonomy principles; market efficiency; fiscal pragmatism
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users exit victim set entirely; third parties enter victim set via externalities (DUI, secondhand exposure) (ε_mod); legal industry emerges as new beneficiary; state becomes revenue collector via taxation; black market collapses or persists in gray areas

axiom_contradictions.basis: Prohibition axiom (state authority derives from duty to enforce moral order against individual vice) directly contradicts legalization axiom (state authority limited to third-party harm prevention, individual autonomy supreme). No coherent framework holds both: either the state has moral enforcement authority or it does not.

Prohibition axiom (use is moral transgression warranting punishment) contradicts harm-reduction axiom (use is health condition warranting medical support without moral judgment). A framework cannot simultaneously classify the same behavior as crime requiring punishment and illness requiring care.
